## Fitting several curves {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
QUESTION: how could we fit this model, one spline per input?

Two minutes. Expected: one curve at a time, each fitted to what the others leave; reveal the algorithm. Legacy "Backfitting algorithm" below the pause, with the intercept and the centering step written in: centering keeps the constants from drifting between components, since only their sum is determined.
:::

::: {.ask}
We know how to fit a spline to one input: least squares on its basis matrix. How could we fit a model with a curve for each of several inputs?
:::

. . .

::: {.fragment}
<h3>Backfitting algorithm</h3>

1. Set $\hat \beta_0 = \bar y$ and start with some initial estimates $\hat f_j$, e.g. $\hat f_j = 0$ or from `y ~ x_j`

2. Iterate over $j$, updating $\hat f_j$ by fitting `r_j ~ x_j` where the partial residual $\mathbf r_j = \mathbf y - \hat \beta_0 - \sum_{k \neq j} \hat f_k(\mathbf x_k)$ is computed using the current fits for all the other predictors; then center $\hat f_j$ (subtract its mean over the data)

3. Repeat until "convergence" (some stopping rule)
:::

## Backfitting and partialling out {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
Line by line: the update is a one-column least-squares slope of the partial residual; a fixed point satisfies both normal equations; that is least squares, whose coefficients the partialling-out theorem describes. With standardized inputs of correlation rho, each sweep multiplies the distance to least squares by rho squared: the next slide shows what that looks like.
:::

Two centered inputs and lines for components, $\hat f_j(x) = \beta_j x$. Step 2 for $j = 1$ regresses the partial residual on $\mathbf x_1$:
$$
\beta_1 \leftarrow \frac{\mathbf x_1^T(\mathbf y - \beta_2 \mathbf x_2)}{\mathbf x_1^T \mathbf x_1}, \qquad
\beta_2 \leftarrow \frac{\mathbf x_2^T(\mathbf y - \beta_1 \mathbf x_1)}{\mathbf x_2^T \mathbf x_2}
$$

. . .

The loop can stop only where both hold: $\mathbf x_j^T(\mathbf y - \beta_1 \mathbf x_1 - \beta_2 \mathbf x_2) = 0$ for $j = 1, 2$. These are the normal equations: the fixed point is least squares

::: {.retrieval}
Partialling-out theorem: the coefficient on $\mathbf x_2$ is $\tilde{\mathbf x}_2^T \mathbf y / \tilde{\mathbf x}_2^T \tilde{\mathbf x}_2$, the slope on what is left of $\mathbf x_2$ after $\mathbf x_1$ has explained what it can.
:::

With a smoother in place of each line, the same loop fits an additive model: each curve fitted to what the others leave

## Backfitting on the films

```{r}
#| label: backfit-films
#| include: false
# Backfitting by hand: smoothing splines (8 effective parameters each) for length and year, a slope for Short.
smooth_c <- function(x, r) { p <- predict(smooth.spline(x, r, df = 8), x)$y; p - mean(p) }
y_bf <- mv_train$rating; b0_bf <- mean(y_bf); short_c <- mv_train$Short - mean(mv_train$Short)
f_len <- f_yr <- f_sh <- rep(0, nrow(mv_train)); beta_sh <- numeric(100); len_iter <- list()
for (k in 1:100) {
  f_len <- smooth_c(mv_train$length, y_bf - b0_bf - f_yr - f_sh)
  f_yr  <- smooth_c(mv_train$year,   y_bf - b0_bf - f_len - f_sh)
  r_sh <- y_bf - b0_bf - f_len - f_yr; beta_sh[k] <- sum(short_c * r_sh) / sum(short_c^2); f_sh <- beta_sh[k] * short_c
  len_iter[[k]] <- tibble(sweep = k, length = mv_train$length, curve = f_len)
}
settle <- which(abs(beta_sh - beta_sh[100]) < 0.01 * abs(beta_sh[100]))[1]
cor_ls <- cor(mv_train$length, mv_train$Short)
```

::: {.notes}
Smoothing splines with 8 effective parameters each (smooth.spline, df = 8), not mgcv's penalties, so the curves differ a little from the last fit. Length and Short have correlation `r round(cor_ls, 2)`, so rho squared would suggest fast convergence; but the length curve can bend to mimic the Short flag, which a line cannot, so the sweeps shrink the distance far more slowly. The coefficient is within 1% of its final value after `r settle` sweeps.
:::

```{r}
#| label: backfit-films-plot
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-align: center
sel <- c(1, 3, 10, 30, 100)
p_len <- bind_rows(len_iter[sel]) |>
  ggplot(aes(length, curve, group = sweep, colour = sweep)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(trans = "log10", breaks = sel, end = 0.9) +
  labs(x = "length (minutes)", y = "length curve")
p_sh <- tibble(sweep = 1:100, beta = beta_sh) |>
  ggplot(aes(sweep, beta)) + geom_line(colour = v_dark, linewidth = 1.2) + scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "sweep (log axis)", y = "Short coefficient")
p_len + p_sh + plot_layout(widths = c(1.5, 1))
```

Length, year and Short on the training films, starting from zero. Length and Short are closely related: each sweep moves a little more of the shorts' higher ratings from the length curve to the Short coefficient, which settles after about `r 10 * round(settle / 10)` sweeps

## Backfitting, more generally

::: {.notes}
Gauss-Seidel solves a linear system one unknown at a time, using the latest values; with exact minimization in each block on a least-squares problem it is the same as coordinate descent. Gram-Schmidt is ESL's "regression by successive orthogonalization" (Algorithm 3.1): the last coefficient is the slope on the last input's residual, the partialling-out theorem again. With a smoother that is not least squares, such as loess, backfitting and residual-on-residual give different estimates.
:::

**Any number of inputs.** With one coefficient per input, each update minimizes the RSS over that coefficient with the others held fixed: **coordinate descent** (Gauss–Seidel, in numerical linear algebra). It converges to least squares: in one sweep for orthogonal inputs, slowly for strongly related ones

**Gram–Schmidt** partials out the other way round: it residualizes each *input* on the ones before it, once. Backfitting leaves the inputs alone and residualizes $\mathbf y$, again and again

**Partialling out with flexible fits.** Residualize both $\mathbf y$ and $\mathbf x_j$ on the other inputs, with any regression method, then regress residual on residual: double machine learning, later in the course

### Part 2: plots for other models

## Can additivity/GAMs be *importantly wrong*?

::: {.notes}
Legacy slide, the calculus half. The causality half is later in the course, where a model's curve is compared with an effect.
:::

Interpretation: think carefully about **calculus** and **causality** (causality: later in the course). To simplify let's consider the identity link function (rather than e.g. logistic regression, those cases are more complicated)

#### Calculus

Does the CEF really decompose into additive terms?  Is this approximation good:

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial x_j} \mathbb E[Y | \mathbf X] \approx g(x_j)
$$
Or does the relationship between the average of $Y$ and $x_j$ vary depending on the value of another predictor $x_k$?

## Interactions in the movies data

```{r}
#| label: movies-decades
#| include: false
mv_dec <- mv_train |> mutate(decade = 10 * (year %/% 10))
cor_dec <- mv_dec |> filter(Short == 0) |> group_by(decade) |>
  summarise(r = round(cor(length, rating), 2), .groups = "drop")
```

::: {.notes}
Legacy "Interactions" and "Misspecification", merged. Decades, not years (too few films in one year), and non-shorts only (the shorts put a dip near an hour in every decade). The correlation of length with rating goes from `r cor_dec$r[cor_dec$decade == 1950]` in the 1950s to `r cor_dec$r[cor_dec$decade == 2000]` in the 2000s: a raw correlation, not a fitted interaction.
:::

If the slope in length changes with year, the derivative of $\mathbb E[\text{rating} \mid \text{length}, \text{year}]$ in length depends on year too, and an additive model is misspecified. Non-shorts, by decade:

```{r}
#| label: movies-interaction
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.1
#| fig-align: center
mv_dec |> filter(decade >= 1950, Short == 0) |>
  mutate(decade = paste0(decade, "s")) |>
  ggplot(aes(length, rating)) + geom_point(alpha = .15, size = 1) +
  geom_smooth(colour = v_blue, se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.3) + facet_wrap(~ decade, nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(60, 120, 180)) +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 16))
```

## Now true model is **not** additive

::: {.notes}
Legacy slides from the interpretation deck, merged. The CEF (conditional expectation function, E[Y | X]) is x_1 squared times cos(pi x_2 / 2): a parabola in x_1 opening up where the cosine is positive and down where it is negative, which average to almost nothing. The legacy text wrote cos(x_2).
:::

```{r}
#| label: int-sim
#| echo: true
f1 <- function(x) x^2
f2 <- function(x) cos(pi * x / 2)
df_int <- tibble(x1 = runif(2000, -1, 1), x2 = runif(2000, -4, 4)) |>
  mutate(y = f1(x1) * f2(x2) + rnorm(2000))
fit_gam_wrong <- gam(y ~ s(x1) + s(x2), data = df_int)
```

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{r}
#| label: int-gam
#| fig-width: 7.4
#| fig-height: 3.2
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 0.6, 0.6), cex = 1.2)
plot(fit_gam_wrong, col = v_blue, shade = TRUE, shade.col = "#31688e33", ylim = c(-1, 1))
```
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
The fitted component for $x_1$ is nearly flat: a parabola opening upward when $\cos(\pi x_2/2) > 0$ and downward when $\cos(\pi x_2/2) < 0$ cancel when averaged over $x_2$

Additivity assumption is now (importantly) wrong
:::
:::

## Plotting one input {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
QUESTION: plot f-hat against x_1: what do we do with x_2?

Two minutes, written, then three answers before the next slide. Expected: fix x_2 at a typical value, its median or mean (one curve); one curve for each unit, at its own x_2; the average of those curves. What each hides here: at the median of x_2 (about 0, where the cosine is 1) the curve opens upward, while for about half the units it opens downward; the average of all the curves is nearly flat.
:::

A forest fitted to these data can hold the interaction, but it has no components: $\hat f(x_1, x_2)$ is one function of both inputs

::: {.ask}
We want a plot of how $\hat f$ depends on $x_1$. What do we do with $x_2$ while we draw it?

Write down one way, and what that plot could hide.
:::

## Partial dependence

::: {.notes}
The answers to the last slide: legacy "What to do about other variables?". Notation from Loftus, Bynum and Hansen (2024), without their prime for the explained units. The PDP is a computation on f-hat: set, leave, predict, average. For an additive f-hat it is the component plus a constant (the other components' averages). Fixing the others at their medians gives a different curve in general.
:::

For models with multiple predictors, partial dependence plots can hide model structure. Options for the other variables:

- Hold other variables fixed (e.g. at medians), `plotmo` default
- Average over them, `pdp` method
- Plot a curve for each observation: individual conditional expectation (ICE), `ice` method

Unit $i$'s inputs with input $j$ set to a value $\tilde x_j$: $\;\tilde{\mathbf x}_{ij} = (x_{i1}, \ldots, \tilde x_j, \ldots, x_{ip})$
$$
\mathrm{ICE}_i:\ \tilde x_j \mapsto \hat f(\tilde{\mathbf x}_{ij}), \qquad
\mathrm{PDP}_j:\ \tilde x_j \mapsto \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^n \hat f(\tilde{\mathbf x}_{ij})
$$

A modified unit may resemble no real unit

## Regression trees + bagging {minutes="1"}

::: {.notes}
Legacy slide, shown twice: first the average alone. A forest on the same data, every input offered at every split (bagging); nodes under 50 units are not split. Flat, like the GAM's x_1 curve on "Now true model is not additive". Does the forest ignore x_1? Go to the next slide.
:::

```{r}
#| label: rf-ice
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
fit_rf <- randomForest(y ~ x1 + x2, data = df_int, ntree = 300, mtry = 2, nodesize = 50)
ice_x1 <- partial(fit_rf, pred.var = "x1", ice = TRUE, train = df_sub)
```

```{r}
#| label: rf-pdp-plot
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-align: center
# The code shown above, on 100 of the 2,000 units, and the plot.
fit_rf <- randomForest(y ~ x1 + x2, data = df_int, ntree = 300, mtry = 2, nodesize = 50)
df_sub <- df_int |> slice_sample(n = 100) |> mutate(yhat.id = row_number(), sign = if_else(f2(x2) > 0, "positive", "negative"))
ice_x1 <- partial(fit_rf, pred.var = "x1", ice = TRUE, train = as.data.frame(df_sub[, c("x1", "x2")]), grid.resolution = 30) |>
  as_tibble() |> left_join(df_sub |> select(yhat.id, sign), by = "yhat.id")
pdp_x1 <- ice_x1 |> group_by(x1) |> summarise(yhat = mean(yhat), .groups = "drop")
ice_ylim <- range(ice_x1$yhat)
ggplot(pdp_x1, aes(x1, yhat)) +
  geom_line(colour = "black", linewidth = 1.8) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = ice_ylim) + labs(x = "x1", y = "prediction")
```

Black: the PDP, the forest's prediction averaged over the 100 units with $x_1$ set and $x_2$ left at each unit's value. Nearly flat

## Regression trees + bagging

::: {.notes}
The same slide with the ICE curves. Solid teal: units with cos(pi x_2 / 2) > 0; dashed orange: < 0. The GAM's x_1 curve was flat too, but the GAM has no interaction to hide; only the ICE curves tell the two apart.
:::

```{r}
#| label: rf-ice-shown-again
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
fit_rf <- randomForest(y ~ x1 + x2, data = df_int, ntree = 300, mtry = 2, nodesize = 50)
ice_x1 <- partial(fit_rf, pred.var = "x1", ice = TRUE, train = df_sub)
```

```{r}
#| label: rf-ice-plot
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-align: center
# The same forest, curves and axes as on the last slide, with the ICE curves added.
ggplot(ice_x1, aes(x1, yhat)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = yhat.id, colour = sign, linetype = sign), alpha = 0.6, linewidth = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_line(data = pdp_x1, colour = "black", linewidth = 1.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(positive = v_teal, negative = m_orange)) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(positive = "solid", negative = "dashed")) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = ice_ylim) + labs(x = "x1", y = "prediction")
```

Thin: one curve per unit (ICE), solid where $\cos(\pi x_2/2) > 0$, dashed where it is negative. The forest fitted the interaction; the average hides it

## Split search

```{r}
#| label: split-curve
#| include: false
# Every legal cutoff: between two consecutive sorted values that differ.
rss_curve <- function(x, y) {
  o <- order(x); xs <- x[o]; ys <- y[o]; n <- length(y)
  S <- cumsum(ys); Q <- cumsum(ys^2); i <- 1:(n - 1)
  i <- i[xs[i] < xs[i + 1]]
  tibble(cut = (xs[i] + xs[i + 1]) / 2,
         rss = (Q[i] - S[i]^2 / i) + ((Q[n] - Q[i]) - (S[n] - S[i])^2 / (n - i)))
}
rc <- rss_curve(mv_train$length, mv_train$rating)
best_cut <- rc |> slice_min(rss, n = 1)
other_cut <- rc |> filter(cut < 90) |> slice_min(rss, n = 1)
root_rss <- sum((mv_train$rating - mean(mv_train$rating))^2)
```

::: {.notes}
Every cutoff between two films of different length, scored by the RSS of predicting each side's mean: the best is `r best_cut$cut` minutes, which takes the RSS from `r format(round(root_rss), big.mark = ",")` (the dotted line, no split) to `r format(round(best_cut$rss), big.mark = ",")`, a fall of `r round(100 * (1 - best_cut$rss / root_rss))`%; the other dip is at `r other_cut$cut` minutes. One question about one input explains little. Compare with the room's cutoffs.
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="56%"}
```{r}
#| label: split-search
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 4.4
ggplot(rc, aes(cut, rss)) +
  geom_line(colour = v_blue, linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = root_rss, linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = best_cut$cut, colour = m_pink, linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = best_cut$cut - 12, y = best_cut$rss + 0.1 * (root_rss - best_cut$rss), hjust = 1, size = 6, colour = m_pink,
           label = paste0("best: ", best_cut$cut, " minutes")) +
  labs(x = "cutoff in length (minutes)", y = "RSS of the two means")
```
:::
::: {.column width="44%"}
Every cutoff between two films, scored by the RSS when each side predicts its own mean

Each side of a split is a **leaf** (until it is split again)

Then every input; keep the best; then **recurse** into each leaf. Greedy: each split is the best *now*

For a label: the same search, scoring each split by its leaves' **Gini indices** $\sum_k \hat p_k (1 - \hat p_k)$, weighted by leaf size
:::
:::

## Growing and pruning

```{r}
#| label: big-tree
#| include: false
fit_tree <- rpart(rating ~ year + length, data = mv_train,
                  control = rpart.control(cp = 0, minsplit = 2, minbucket = 1))
n_leaves <- sum(fit_tree$frame$var == "<leaf>")
n_pairs <- nrow(distinct(mv_train, year, length))
```

::: {.notes}
Legacy "Complexity and overfitting", "Growing and pruning" and "How to prune a tree", merged. Grown out, rpart gives `r format(n_leaves, big.mark = ",")` leaves for `r format(n_pairs, big.mark = ",")` distinct (year, length) pairs: it cannot split films that share their inputs. In rpart the path is the cptable, cp a rescaled alpha.
:::

Split until no leaf can split, and a tree is like 1-nearest neighbors: `r format(n_leaves, big.mark = ",")` leaves on year and length alone

**Greedy splitting**: each split is the best now, and stopping early can miss a weak split that enables a strong one below it. So grow a large tree

**Overfitting**: then prune. Of the many sub-trees, take only the path of minimizers of
$$RSS(\text{Sub-tree}) + \alpha\, |\text{Sub-tree}|, \qquad \alpha \geq 0$$
and choose $\alpha$, and so a sub-tree, by validation

::: {.retrieval}
$k$ nearest neighbors average the $k$ training points closest to $x_0$; a tree averages those in $x_0$'s leaf, a neighborhood chosen by the data
:::

## Four samples, four trees {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
QUESTION: same method, same films, four different trees: what should we do?

Each tree is grown to depth 2 on a random half of the 5,000 training films. The root question changes between halves, and so do the questions under it. The structures lecture showed the same on the countries, with resamples; some will remember averaging. A minute for the room; the next slide's three strategies are the answers.
:::

```{r}
#| label: unstable-trees
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 3.0
#| fig-align: center
# Genre flags as factors, so that a split prints "Drama=yes", not "Drama>=0.5"; the trees are the same.
mv_train_f <- mv_train |> mutate(across(all_of(genres), function(g) factor(g, levels = 0:1, labels = c("no", "yes"))))
half_trees <- map(1:4, function(b) rpart(f_all, data = slice_sample(mv_train_f, n = 2500),
                                         control = rpart.control(maxdepth = 2, cp = 0, minbucket = 30)))
shawshank <- mv_train_f |> slice_max(votes, n = 1) |> mutate(title = sub("^(.*), The$", "The \\1", title))
pred_shaw <- sapply(half_trees, function(t) predict(t, shawshank))
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(0.7, 1.5, 0.7, 1.5), xpd = NA)
for (t in half_trees) { plot(t, uniform = TRUE, margin = 0.1); text(t, cex = 1.45, digits = 3, pretty = 0) }
```

Depth 2, each on a random half of the training films. *`r shawshank$title`* (rated `r shawshank$rating`): predicted `r paste(sprintf("%.2f", pred_shaw), collapse = ", ")`

::: {.ask}
Same method, same films, four different models. What should we do about this?
:::

## Part 4: three model improvement strategies {.inverse}

::: {.notes}
Compress: three ways to use many trees: average resampled trees, average trees that see random subsets of predictors, or add small trees one at a time. Legacy slide; "at each split" for "when resampling", and the boosting block no longer says what the next model is fitted to: "Adding trees" asks.
:::

Sacrifice simplicity/interpretability for prediction accuracy

Can be used with other models too, not just trees

#### **Bagging**: bootstrap aggregating

- Resample training data, average resulting models

#### **Random forest**: randomly drop predictors

- Randomly drop predictors at each split

#### **Boosting**: add models one at a time

- Each new model is added to the sum of the previous ones

## Bagging: bootstrap aggregating

::: {.notes}
Legacy slide, whole. A bootstrap sample, once, with an example: from rows 1 to 5 a draw might be 2, 2, 4, 5, 1, so row 3 is left out and row 2 counts twice. Row 3 returns on the out-of-bag slide.
:::

**Problem**: a single tree model can have high variance (like many non-smooth or non-regularized models)

1. **Bootstrap**: for each $b = 1, \ldots, B$  resamples (with replacement) of the training data, fit $\hat f^{*b}$ on bootstrap sample $b$

2. **Aggregate**: combine the $B$ models, using majority vote for classification or mean for regression

$$\hat f_\text{bag} = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^B \hat f^{*b}$$

("Smoothing" useful for low-bias, high-variance models)

## Averaging $B$ trees {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
QUESTION: variance of an average of B trees: copies, independent, correlation rho?

Two minutes, written. Expected: tau^2 (no reduction), then tau^2 / B; the third is the next slide. Collect all three first.
:::

Average $B$ trees' predictions at one input $x$

::: {.ask}
What is the variance of their average if the $B$ trees are

- copies of the *same* tree, with variance $\tau^2$?
- independent, each with variance $\tau^2$?
- each with variance $\tau^2$, every pair with correlation $\rho$?
:::

## Correlated-average variance {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
The lecture's proof: count the terms, state, divide by B squared and regroup. Check: rho = 1 gives tau^2, rho = 0 gives tau^2 / B. Given the sample the bootstrap trees are independent, so rho tau^2 is the part of one tree's variance that comes from the sample; more trees cannot remove it.
:::

The variance of a sum is every variance plus every covariance, $B$ terms $\tau^2$ and $B(B - 1)$ terms $\rho\tau^2$: $\;\mathrm{Var}\big(\sum_{b} V_b\big) = B\tau^2 + B(B - 1)\rho\tau^2$

. . .

::: {.leave}
**Correlated-average variance.** $V_1, \ldots, V_B$, each with variance $\tau^2$, every pair with correlation $\rho$:
$$
\mathrm{Var}\Big(\frac1B \sum_{b=1}^B V_b\Big) = \rho\,\tau^2 + (1 - \rho)\,\frac{\tau^2}{B}
$$
:::

**Proof**: divide by $B^2$ and regroup, $\frac{\tau^2}{B} + \frac{B - 1}{B}\rho\tau^2 = \rho\tau^2 + (1 - \rho)\frac{\tau^2}{B}$. Bagging shrinks the second term; $\rho\tau^2$ stays, since bootstrap trees grown from one sample are alike

## Random forest: dropping predictors

::: {.notes}
QUESTION: B is already 300: which term is left, and how could we shrink it?

A minute. Expected: rho tau^2; make the trees less alike. Legacy edits: predictors redrawn at every split, not once per tree; "(typically)". randomForest's default for regression offers p/3 predictors, here 3 of the 9.
:::

::: {.ask}
$B$ is already 300. Which term of the correlated-average variance is left, and how could we make it smaller?
:::

. . .

**Problem**: aggregation does not increase information if the aggregates are highly correlated, e.g. averaging 1000 trees but each one uses the same small set of predictor variables

1. **Drop** predictors randomly, at every split

    e.g. each split chooses among a random $\sqrt{p}$ of the $p$ predictors

2. **Aggregate** models which are now (typically) less correlated, achieving greater variance reduction

## Out-of-bag predictions

::: {.notes}
Legacy slide, with the films. Training MSE uses every tree, including those that had the film in their sample, so it is too low; out of bag, each film is predicted only by the trees that never saw it, close to the tuning score. Once used to choose mtry or the number of trees, it is a validation score, not a test.
:::

- Each bootstrap sample contains some subset of the training data

- Roughly $1/e \approx 0.37$ portion of the training samples will be left out of each bootstrap sample

- Can use these to estimate test error (e.g. instead of $K$-fold cross-validation)

Software implementations may do this automatically

```{r}
#| label: oob
#| output: asis
rf_mv <- randomForest(f_all, data = mv_train, ntree = 300, mtry = 3)   # mtry = 3 is the default for 9 inputs; fixed for LOCO
oob_tab <- tibble(
  score = c("training films, every tree", "training films, out-of-bag trees only", "tuning films", "tuning films, predicting the training mean"),
  mse = c(mse(mv_train$rating, predict(rf_mv, mv_train)), mse(mv_train$rating, predict(rf_mv)),
          mse(mv_tune$rating, predict(rf_mv, mv_tune)), mse(mv_tune$rating, mean(mv_train$rating))))
cat("::: {style=\"font-size: 0.9em\"}\n| A forest on the films, 300 trees | MSE |\n|---|---|\n")
cat(sprintf("| %s | %.2f |\n", oob_tab$score, oob_tab$mse), sep = "")
cat(":::\n")
```

## Adding trees

::: {.notes}
QUESTION: add one small tree to the current fit: what should it predict?

A minute. Expected: the residuals, y minus the current fit; some will say the worst-fit films. The same move as backfitting, which fitted each curve to what the others left.
:::

A forest grows its trees separately and averages them. Now grow them one after another and add them up: after $b$ trees the fit is $\hat f^{(b)}$, the sum so far

::: {.ask}
We may add one small tree to $\hat f^{(b)}$. What should it predict?
:::

## Boosting: iterated fitting on residuals

::: {.notes}
The answer to the last slide. Legacy slide; the ESL link is the current address, and two parentheticals are dropped (assessment information; "maximum inner product", unbounded without a norm constraint). The tree is found greedily, so it approximates the closest small tree.
:::

**Idea**: train models sequentially, decreasing residuals by a small amount each time. Each model contributes something different

Can use "weak learners" (e.g. trees with one split, "stumps") to grow an ensemble model gradually fitting closer to the training data

. . .

#### Relationship with gradient descent

**Gradient descent**: small step in direction of negative gradient

**Boosting**: small step in direction of *weak learner closest to negative gradient*

Instead of computing gradients, we reduce the loss by taking a small step in the direction of a weak learner: a simple, low-cost model

Optional additional reading: [ESL](https://hastie.su.domains/ElemStatLearn/) Chapter 10

## Boosting as gradient descent {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
Derived. What we have: a loss of the n fitted values. What we want: a step that lowers it. The gradient with respect to the fitted values is f - y, so the negative gradient is the residual. Notation: f-hat^(b) is the sum after b rounds, t-hat_b the small tree added at round b. A tree turns the n numbers into a function of x, which is why the step can be applied to new films. gamma is the learning rate; ISLR writes lambda, which this course keeps for the penalty.
:::

Gradient descent moves parameters. Take the $n$ fitted values $f(x_1), \ldots, f(x_n)$ as the parameters, with squared loss $L(f) = \frac12 \sum_{i=1}^n \big(y_i - f(x_i)\big)^2$:
$$
-\frac{\partial L}{\partial f(x_i)} = y_i - f(x_i): \quad \text{the negative gradient is the residual vector}
$$

. . .

A step along it moves only those $n$ values. Fit a small tree to the residuals instead (defined at every $x$), and step along the tree, with **learning rate** $\gamma$:
$$
\hat f^{(0)} = \bar y, \qquad \hat f^{(b)} = \hat f^{(b-1)} + \gamma\, \hat t_b, \qquad \hat t_b \text{ a small tree fitted to } y_i - \hat f^{(b-1)}(x_i)
$$

::: {.retrieval}
Gradient descent, stopped early: the number of steps is a knob. Backfitting replaced a curve; boosting adds a tree, fitted to what the sum leaves.
:::

## Boosting in practice {minutes="1"}

::: {.notes}
Legacy slide, the grid-tuning half cut; the learning rate is gamma, as on the last slide. More trees in a forest settle to an average; more rounds of boosting keep fitting the training data.
:::

#### More tuning parameters

Number of trees/steps $B$, complexity of each tree/model $d$, regularization/learning rate $\gamma$. **Warning**: can now overfit with large $B$ (unlike bagging/r.f.)

Software may choose them automatically. *No guarantee it's reasonable!*

#### Bagging and boosting

Bagging and forests start with large trees, which have high variance individually, and average them to lower the variance. Boosting starts with weak learners like tree stumps, which have high bias individually, and fits iteratively on residuals to lower the bias

## Rounds and learning rate

```{r}
#| label: rounds-curves
#| include: false
X_tr <- as.matrix(mv_train[, inputs]); X_tu <- as.matrix(mv_tune[, inputs])
rounds <- unique(round(10^seq(0, 3, length.out = 40)))
boost_curve <- function(rate) {
  fit <- xgboost(x = X_tr, y = mv_train$rating, nrounds = 1000, learning_rate = rate, max_depth = 2, nthread = 1)
  map_dfr(rounds, function(b) tibble(b = b,
    training = mse(mv_train$rating, predict(fit, X_tr, iteration_range = c(1, b))),
    tuning   = mse(mv_tune$rating,  predict(fit, X_tu, iteration_range = c(1, b)))))
}
bc <- bind_rows(boost_curve(0.3) |> mutate(rate = "0.3"), boost_curve(0.03) |> mutate(rate = "0.03"))
best_round <- bc |> group_by(rate) |> slice_min(tuning, n = 1) |> with(setNames(b, rate))
best_tune <- bc |> group_by(rate) |> summarise(m = min(tuning)) |> with(setNames(round(m, 3), rate))
```

::: {.notes}
xgboost on the films, trees of depth 2, at two learning rates; training and tuning MSE after each number of rounds. With gamma = 0.3 the tuning MSE is lowest at round `r best_round[["0.3"]]` (`r best_tune[["0.3"]]`) and then drifts up; with gamma = 0.03 it is `r if (best_round[["0.03"]] == max(rounds)) "still falling at the last round, 1,000" else paste("lowest at round", best_round[["0.03"]])` (`r best_tune[["0.03"]]`). The mean alone scores `r round(mse(mv_tune$rating, mean(mv_train$rating)), 3)`. Patterns, not guarantees: at a fixed budget of rounds a small rate can underfit. First on the cut order.
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="56%"}
```{r}
#| label: rounds
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 4.4
bc |> pivot_longer(c(training, tuning)) |>
  ggplot(aes(b, value, colour = name, linetype = rate)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_x_log10() + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(1.4, 2.6)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(training = v_blue, tuning = m_pink), name = NULL) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(`0.3` = 1, `0.03` = 3), name = expression(gamma)) +
  labs(x = "rounds B (log axis)", y = "MSE") + theme(legend.position = "top")
```
:::
::: {.column width="44%"}
**Rounds $B$.** Training error keeps falling; tuning error turns. Stopping there is early stopping, as for gradient descent

**Learning rate $\gamma$.** Smaller steps, more of them; often a lower minimum, not always

**Depth.** How many inputs one tree can combine (next)
:::
:::

## Tree depth and interactions {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
QUESTION: one split for x_1 x_2? how many for x_1 ... x_p?

Two minutes. One split on x_1 at any c: each side averages x_1 x_2 over x_2, whose mean is 0, so both leaves predict 0 and the split gains nothing; the same for x_2, so greedy splitting stops at the root. A split on x_1 and then on x_2 in each child gives the quadrant means, plus or minus 1/4. For x_1 ... x_p a leaf predicts 0 unless it restricts every input: depth p, 2^p - 1 splits, none of which helps on its own.
:::

::: {.ask}
Can a tree with one split fit $f(x_1, x_2) = x_1 x_2$ well? Hint: assume the inputs are independent, both $\mathrm{Unif}[-1, 1]$

How many splits would we want for $f = x_1 \cdots x_p$?
:::

. . .

A stump asks one question, so a sum of stumps is a sum of one-input functions: an **additive** model. Depth $d$: interactions of up to $d$ inputs

A boosted model is additive in trees, not in the predictors

## {.inverse .center}

::: {.notes}
Compress: what did the forest use? Permutation importance shuffles one input; LOCO refits without it.
:::

### Part 5: feature importance

## Feature/variable "importance"

::: {.notes}
Legacy slide, now light (it was dark), with the forest from the out-of-bag slide. Split improvement is randomForest's IncNodePurity; permutation is on the tuning films, the forest unchanged, ten shuffles each. Each measure is shown as a share of its total over the nine inputs, so the two can share an axis.
:::

- Which predictors are *used most* by the model?
- Does not necessarily tell us about **causation** (none of these methods do)

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
#### Tree-specific importance

Sum the RSS decrease of every split on $x_j$ within a tree, then average over trees

#### Permutation importance

Permute values of predictor $x_j$. How much does the accuracy of the model decrease?
$$\mathrm{PI}_j = \widehat{\mathrm{Err}}(\hat f, x_j \text{ permuted}) - \widehat{\mathrm{Err}}(\hat f)$$
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r}
#| label: importance
#| fig-width: 5.0
#| fig-height: 3.15
base_tune <- mse(mv_tune$rating, predict(rf_mv, mv_tune))
pi_j <- sapply(inputs, function(v) mean(replicate(10, {
  d <- mv_tune; d[[v]] <- sample(d[[v]]); mse(mv_tune$rating, predict(rf_mv, d)) })) - base_tune)
split_j <- importance(rf_mv)[inputs, "IncNodePurity"]
tibble(input = factor(inputs, levels = inputs[order(split_j)]),
       `split improvement` = split_j / sum(split_j), permutation = pi_j / sum(pi_j)) |>
  pivot_longer(-input, names_to = "measure") |>
  ggplot(aes(value, input, colour = measure, shape = measure)) + geom_point(size = 3.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`split improvement` = v_dark, permutation = m_pink), name = NULL) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`split improvement` = 15, permutation = 17), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "share of the measure's total", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", legend.margin = ggplot2::margin(0, 0, -8, 0), axis.text.y = element_text(size = 13))
```

Each has pros/cons, no satisfactory answer for dependence
:::
:::

## Permutation and extrapolation

```{r}
#| label: permute-counts
#| include: false
perm <- mv_tune |> mutate(length = sample(length))
odd <- function(d) c(long_short = sum(d$Short == 1 & d$length > 60), short_other = sum(d$Short == 0 & d$length < 40))
n_short <- sum(mv_tune$Short == 1)
odd_perm <- odd(perm); odd_tune <- odd(mv_tune); odd_train <- odd(mv_train)
```

::: {.notes}
The tuning films, length shuffled once. Hooker, Mentch and Zhou (2021): with dependent inputs, shuffling puts weight where there are few data, in importance and in partial dependence alike; a PDP sets length on every film, shorts included.
:::

```{r}
#| label: permute-length
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 2.7
#| fig-align: center
bind_rows(mv_tune |> mutate(data = "tuning films"),
          perm |> mutate(data = "length permuted")) |>
  mutate(data = fct_inorder(data), kind = if_else(Short == 1, "short", "non-short")) |>
  ggplot(aes(length, kind, colour = kind)) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.25, width = 0, alpha = 0.35, size = 1.2, show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ data) + scale_colour_manual(values = c(`non-short` = v_blue, short = m_pink)) +
  labs(x = "length (minutes)", y = NULL) + theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 16))
```

Shuffling length keeps each film's other inputs: `r odd_perm[["long_short"]]` of the `r n_short` shorts now run over an hour, and `r odd_perm[["short_other"]]` non-shorts under 40 minutes. Before: `r odd_tune[["long_short"]]` and `r odd_tune[["short_other"]]`; in the 5,000 training films, `r odd_train[["long_short"]]` and `r odd_train[["short_other"]]`

The forest's predictions there rest on almost no data, and permutation importance averages over them (Hooker, Mentch and Zhou 2021)

## Permutation with correlated inputs

```{r}
#| label: biv-perm
#| include: false
n_biv <- 400; rho_biv <- -0.8
b1 <- rnorm(n_biv); b2 <- rho_biv * b1 + sqrt(1 - rho_biv^2) * rnorm(n_biv)
biv <- tibble(x1 = b1, x2 = b2); biv_perm <- tibble(x1 = b1, x2 = sample(b2))
biv_lims <- c(-3.6, 3.6)
biv_kde <- MASS::kde2d(biv$x1, biv$x2, n = 120, lims = c(biv_lims, biv_lims))
biv_grid <- expand_grid(x2 = biv_kde$y, x1 = biv_kde$x) |> mutate(z = as.vector(t(biv_kde$z)))
biv_breaks <- c(0.002, 0.01, 0.03, 0.06, 0.1, 0.15, 0.3)
dens_at <- function(x, y) biv_kde$z[cbind(pmax(findInterval(x, biv_kde$x), 1), pmax(findInterval(y, biv_kde$y), 1))]
low_perm <- mean(dens_at(biv_perm$x1, biv_perm$x2) < 0.01); low_data <- mean(dens_at(biv$x1, biv$x2) < 0.01)
```

::: {.notes}
Away from the films: x_1, x_2 standard normal with correlation -0.8. Permuting x_2 keeps both marginals and breaks the dependence, so the pairs come from the product of the marginals. Both panels shade the density estimated from the data on the left. A model fitted to the left panel has seen almost nothing where many right-panel points fall.
:::

```{r}
#| label: biv-perm-plot
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-align: center
biv_panel <- function(d, title) ggplot() +
  geom_contour_filled(data = biv_grid, aes(x1, x2, z = z), breaks = biv_breaks, alpha = 0.85, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(data = d, aes(x1, x2), size = 1.2, alpha = 0.7, colour = "#1f1f1f") +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "mako", direction = -1, begin = 0.15) +
  coord_equal(xlim = biv_lims, ylim = biv_lims, expand = FALSE) + labs(title = title, x = "x1", y = "x2") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 17))
biv_panel(biv, "the data, and their density") + biv_panel(biv_perm, "x2 permuted, the same density")
```

Where the data's density is below 0.01: `r round(100 * low_perm)`% of the permuted points, `r round(100 * low_data)`% of the data

## Leave one covariate out

::: {.notes}
Ten more forests, mtry = 3 as in the full one: one per input left out, one without length and Short; all scored on the tuning films. Permutation is larger for every input that matters, with or without extrapolation: for an additive f with independent inputs, permuting x_j adds 2 Var f_j(X_j) to the error, refitting without it Var f_j(X_j). Two questions: how much the fitted model relies on x_j; what the method loses without it. The reading's LOFO.
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r}
#| label: loco
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 4.6
refit_without <- function(drop) {
  fit <- randomForest(reformulate(setdiff(inputs, drop), "rating"), data = mv_train, ntree = 300, mtry = 3)
  mse(mv_tune$rating, predict(fit, mv_tune)) - base_tune
}
loco_j <- sapply(inputs, refit_without)
loco_pair <- refit_without(c("length", "Short"))
tibble(input = inputs, permutation = pi_j, LOCO = loco_j) |>
  pivot_longer(-input, names_to = "importance") |>
  mutate(input = fct_reorder(input, value, .fun = max)) |>
  ggplot(aes(value, input, colour = importance, shape = importance)) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(LOCO = v_blue, permutation = m_pink), name = NULL) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(LOCO = 16, permutation = 17), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "increase in tuning MSE", y = NULL) + theme(legend.position = "top")
```
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
Refit without input $j$, with the same settings; score on the same held-out films (Lei et al. 2018):
$$\mathrm{LOCO}_j = \widehat{\mathrm{Err}}\big(\hat f^{(-j)}\big) - \widehat{\mathrm{Err}}(\hat f)$$

No extrapolation from permuting; any method, at the cost of $p$ refits

Length and Short together: `r sprintf("%.2f", loco_pair)`, more than length alone and Short alone added up (`r sprintf("%.2f", loco_j[["length"]])` + `r sprintf("%.2f", loco_j[["Short"]])`). Each stands in for part of the other
:::
:::

But consider, [Alfred North Whitehead](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/41568) wrote (1911):

## Conclusion {.inverse}

::: {.notes}
Compress: an additive model fits one curve per input, each to what the others leave; a plot of one input works best for additive models and can mislead otherwise; trees ask greedy questions, forests average them, boosting adds them; importance asks how much the model suffers when a feature is scrambled or left out.
:::

#### Additive models

One curve per input, each fitted to what the others leave: partialling out, one input at a time

#### Partial dependence

A plot of one input at a time, works most naturally with additive models, can be importantly wrong otherwise

#### Trees and ensembles

Greedy questions, pruned by validation. Bagging and forests average trees to lower variance; boosting adds small trees, gradient descent on the fitted values

#### Feature importance

How much does the model suffer if a feature is scrambled (permuted) or left out before fitting?
